results.title: Things to Do in Shibuya (2026): Shibuya Sky, the Crossing & Where to Eat | Self Guide Japan
results.content:
The bronze statue honors Hachiko, an Akita dog born in 1923 in Odate who met Professor Hidesaburo Ueno at Shibuya Station. The professor died suddenly in 1925, and Hachiko kept coming back to the station to wait for him for nearly ten years. Locals still use the statue as a meeting point, and visitors queue for photos, so the line is slow on weekends. Take your picture, then step aside. Hachiko's final spot in the rebuilt square is still being decided, so the statue may move again before 2034. [...] | Place | Cost | Hours |

This Shibuya landmark right next to Shibuya Scramble Crossing, is a popular photo spot with a constant line of tourists, so be sure to visit in the quieter morning hours!
②         MIYASHITA PARK "SHIBUYA HACHI COMPASS"
Also in Shibuya, another unique Hachiko sculpture is in the rooftop park of the retail complex RAYARD MIYASHITA PARK. As we imagine the true focus of Hachiko's skyward gaze, this photogenic spot tugs at our heartstrings. 💕 [...] Not only at Shibuya Station!? 3 deeply moving Hachiko statues! 🐶
All Japanese people know the touching story of Hachiko, the loyal Akita dog who continued to wait at Shibuya Station, unaware that his owner had passed away. Today, let’s look at some statues to this faithful 4-legged friend in Tokyo!
①        The Hachiko Statue in front of Shibuya Station [...] - Andrew Chapman: I was thinking of Hachi today 😔
- Owen Wylde: Only saw thew one near Shibuya Eki. That means I need to return.
- Toby "Wan Kenobi" Blanco: We visited all three statues on our recent trip to Japan, as well as National Museum of Nature and Science, AND the cemetery where Dr. Ueno is buried alongside Hachiko's ashes.
- Cet GDbarraza: I did know about the others. It was so emotional seeing Hachiko at the Shibuya Station 🥹

  + Enjoy a contrast of old Shibuya at Nonbei Yokocho [...] > TIP: Can you find the “new” Hachiko meeting point in the photo below?

### Give the Hachiko Statue a pat on his head

Tokyo’s most beloved dog, Hachiko, has been immortalised in this bronze statue just outside Shibuya Station. Have you heard his story?

Known as Japan’s most loyal pet (hence his name Chūken Hachikō 忠犬ハチ公 in Japanese), the statue was made in memory of an Akita Inu dog who would patiently wait for his owner to return from work at Shibuya Station each day during the 1930’s. [...] Despite its enormous length, thousands upon thousands of people walk past this mural daily without realising, it is hiding very well in plain sight.

Known by locals as Japan’s Guernica, the Myth of Tomorrow was created in 1969 and depicts the horror and destruction caused by allied nuclear blasts that devastated Hiroshima & Nagasaki during WWII.
